Content:
Recall that when the characteristic equation of a second-order linear homogeneous recurrence relation has two distinct real roots [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: a_n = A \cdot \lambda_1^n + B \cdot \lambda_2^n.]

Content:
As it turns out, this also works in cases where [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] are complex.

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to solve the following recurrence relation:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n} = 6a_{n-1} - 34a_{n-2}]

Content:
Assuming [MATH: a_n=\lambda^n,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: a_{n-1}= \lambda^{n-1},\qquad a_{n-2}= \lambda^{n-2}.]

Content:
Substituting the above into our recurrence relation gives
[MATH: λ^{n}|= 6λ^{n − 1} − 34λ^{n − 2}]

Content:
which can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: λ^{n} − 6λ^{n − 1} + 34λ^{n − 2}|= 0; λ^{n − 2}(λ^{2} − 6λ + 34)|= 0]

Content:
The characteristic equation is

Content:
[MATH: \lambda^2-6\lambda + 34 = 0.]

Content:
This equation can be solved by completing the square:

Content:
[MATH: λ^{2} − 6λ + 34|= 0; (λ^{2} − 6λ + 9) − 9 + 34|= 0; (λ − 3)^{2} + 25|= 0; (λ − 3)^{2}|= − 25; λ − 3|= ± 5\textrm{i}; λ|= 3 ± 5\textrm{i}]

Content:
Therefore, the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: a_n = C \cdot (3 + 5\textrm{i})^n + D \cdot (3 - 5\textrm{i})^n,]

Content:
where [MATH: C] and [MATH: D] are complex conjugate arbitrary constants.

Content:
Suppose that the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous recurrence relation has the complex roots

Content:
[MATH: \lambda_1 = a + \textrm{i}b, \qquad \lambda_2 = a - \textrm{i}b.]

Content:
Since the characteristic equation typically has real coefficients, the roots [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] are complex conjugates.

Content:
The general solution to the recurrence relation is

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= Cλ_{1}^{n} + Dλ_{2}^{n}; = C(a + \textrm{i}b)^{n} + D(a − \textrm{i}b)^{n},]

Content:
where the constants [MATH: C] and [MATH: D] are complex conjugates.

Content:
This solution might seem strange as recurrence relations usually involve real numbers only. Is it possible to express this general solution using only real numbers?

Content:
To answer this, suppose we express our solutions [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] in polar form:

Content:
[MATH: λ_{1} = r(\cos θ + \textrm{i}\sin θ), λ_{2} = r(\cos θ − \textrm{i}\sin θ)]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: r = |\lambda_1|, \qquad \theta = \arg(\lambda_1).]

Content:
Therefore, using De Moivre's theorem, we can write the general solution to the recurrence relation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= Cλ_{1}^{n} + Dλ_{2}^{n}; = C[r(\cos θ + \textrm{i}\sin θ)]^{n} + D[r(\cos (θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (θ))]^{n}; = C[r^{n}(\cos (nθ) + \textrm{i}\sin (nθ))] + D[r^{n}(\cos (nθ) − \textrm{i}\sin (nθ))]; = r^{n}((C + D)\cos (nθ) + \textrm{i}(C − D)\sin (nθ))]

Content:
Finally, if we define the real constants [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] as

Content:
[MATH: A = C+D, \qquad B = \textrm i(C-D),]
we obtain the general solution

Content:
[MATH: a_n = r^n \left( A \cos\left(n\theta\right) + B \sin\left(n\theta\right) \right).]

Content:
Thus, we have managed to write the general solution in terms of real numbers only.

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that when the characteristic equation of a second-order linear homogeneous recurrence relation has two distinct real roots [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2,] the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: a_n = A \cdot \lambda_1^n + B \cdot \lambda_2^n.]

Content:
As it turns out, this also works in cases where [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] are complex.

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to solve the following recurrence relation:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n} = 6a_{n-1} - 34a_{n-2}]

Content:
Assuming [MATH: a_n=\lambda^n,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: a_{n-1}= \lambda^{n-1},\qquad a_{n-2}= \lambda^{n-2}.]

Content:
Substituting the above into our recurrence relation gives
[MATH: λ^{n}|= 6λ^{n − 1} − 34λ^{n − 2}]

Content:
which can be written as follows:

Content:
[MATH: λ^{n} − 6λ^{n − 1} + 34λ^{n − 2}|= 0; λ^{n − 2}(λ^{2} − 6λ + 34)|= 0]

Content:
The characteristic equation is

Content:
[MATH: \lambda^2-6\lambda + 34 = 0.]

Content:
This equation can be solved by completing the square:

Content:
[MATH: λ^{2} − 6λ + 34|= 0; (λ^{2} − 6λ + 9) − 9 + 34|= 0; (λ − 3)^{2} + 25|= 0; (λ − 3)^{2}|= − 25; λ − 3|= ± 5\textrm{i}; λ|= 3 ± 5\textrm{i}]

Content:
Therefore, the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: a_n = C \cdot (3 + 5\textrm{i})^n + D \cdot (3 - 5\textrm{i})^n,]

Content:
where [MATH: C] and [MATH: D] are complex conjugate arbitrary constants.

Item 2 — Example: Finding and Solving a Characteristic Equation

Explanation:
Assuming [MATH: a_n=\lambda^n,] we obtain

[MATH: a_{n-1}= \lambda^{n-1},\qquad a_{n-2}= \lambda^{n-2}.]

Substituting the above into our recurrence relation gives
[MATH: λ^{n}|= − 8λ^{n − 1} − 20λ^{n − 2}]

which can be written as follows:

[MATH: λ^{n} + 8λ^{n − 1} + 20λ^{n − 2}|= 0; λ^{n − 2}(λ^{2} + 8λ + 20)|= 0]

The characteristic equation is

[MATH: \lambda^2+8\lambda + 20 = 0.]

This equation can be solved by completing the square:

[MATH: λ^{2} + 8λ + 20|= 0; (λ^{2} + 8λ + 16) − 16 + 20|= 0; (λ + 4)^{2} + 4|= 0; (λ + 4)^{2}|= − 4; λ + 4|= ± 2\textrm{i}; λ|= − 4 ± 2\textrm{i}]

Item 5 — Tutorial: Simplifying the General Solution Using Complex Numbers in Polar Form

Content:
Suppose that the characteristic equation of a second-order homogeneous recurrence relation has the complex roots

Content:
[MATH: \lambda_1 = a + \textrm{i}b, \qquad \lambda_2 = a - \textrm{i}b.]

Content:
Since the characteristic equation typically has real coefficients, the roots [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] are complex conjugates.

Content:
The general solution to the recurrence relation is

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= Cλ_{1}^{n} + Dλ_{2}^{n}; = C(a + \textrm{i}b)^{n} + D(a − \textrm{i}b)^{n},]

This solution might seem strange as recurrence relations usually involve real numbers only. Is it possible to express this general solution using only real numbers?

To answer this, suppose we express our solutions [MATH: \lambda_1] and [MATH: \lambda_2] in polar form:

Content:
[MATH: λ_{1} = r(\cos θ + \textrm{i}\sin θ), λ_{2} = r(\cos θ − \textrm{i}\sin θ)]

Content:
where

Content:
[MATH: r = |\lambda_1|, \qquad \theta = \arg(\lambda_1).]

Content:
Therefore, using De Moivre's theorem, we can write the general solution to the recurrence relation as follows:

Content:
[MATH: a_{n}|= Cλ_{1}^{n} + Dλ_{2}^{n}; = C[r(\cos θ + \textrm{i}\sin θ)]^{n} + D[r(\cos (θ) − \textrm{i}\sin (θ))]^{n}; = C[r^{n}(\cos (nθ) + \textrm{i}\sin (nθ))] + D[r^{n}(\cos (nθ) − \textrm{i}\sin (nθ))]; = r^{n}((C + D)\cos (nθ) + \textrm{i}(C − D)\sin (nθ))]

Finally, if we define the real constants [MATH: A] and [MATH: B] as

Content:
[MATH: A = C+D, \qquad B = \textrm i(C-D),]
we obtain the general solution

Content:
[MATH: a_n = r^n \left( A \cos\left(n\theta\right) + B \sin\left(n\theta\right) \right).]

Content:
Thus, we have managed to write the general solution in terms of real numbers only.
